lead: Most machines move in one of two simple ways. A lift car slides up its shaft, and every bolt of the car has the same velocity and the same acceleration. A ceiling-fan blade spins about a fixed shaft, and every point of the blade travels a circle about that shaft; the farther a point is from the shaft, the faster it moves. This chapter gives the kinematics of both motions. It defines angular displacement, angular velocity and angular acceleration for fixed-axis rotation, then links them to the ordinary linear velocity and acceleration of a point at radius r. Every later dynamics calculation for wheels, shafts and rotors starts here.
prereq: You need: particle kinematics from Unit 5 (rectilinear and curvilinear motion, tangential and normal components) and comfortable use of angles measured in radians.

blocks.text: A rigid body is a collection of particles in which the distance between any two particles never changes. No real body is perfectly rigid, but a steel shaft or a concrete beam deforms so little that the model works.

Translation is motion in which every line drawn on the body keeps its direction. Every point then has the same velocity and the same acceleration at a given instant. A lift car, a train on a straight track and a block sliding down an incline all translate. A chair on a Ferris wheel also translates, because it stays upright while its centre moves on a circle; the body itself does not turn.

Fixed-axis rotation is motion in which every point of the body travels a circle whose centre lies on one fixed line, the axis of rotation. Points lying on the axis do not move at all. A fan blade, a door on its hinges and a flywheel on a shaft rotate about a fixed axis. Each point only changes its position along its own circle, so one angle describes the whole body. Some syllabi call this 'rotation about a fixed axis'.
Choose a sign convention once and keep it: say anticlockwise is positive and clockwise is negative. A spin that slows down then has angular acceleration of the opposite sign to its angular velocity.

Fix a reference line in space and let θ be the angle a radius of the body makes with it. θ is the angular displacement, in radians (rad). One full turn is 2π rad. One radian is the angle for which the arc length equals the radius, so an arc of length s on a circle of radius r subtends θ = s/r.
Angular velocity ω is the rate of change of θ, and angular acceleration α is the rate of change of ω. Both belong to the body as a whole: every point shares the same θ, ω and α.

blocks.where: θ is the angular displacement (rad); t is time (s); ω is the angular velocity (rad/s); α is the angular acceleration (rad/s²).

blocks.text: When α is constant, three equations link the quantities, exactly as their rectilinear twins do.
ω = ω₀ + αt    θ = ω₀t + ½αt²    ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ
blocks.where: ω₀ is the angular velocity at t = 0 (rad/s); ω is the angular velocity at time t (rad/s); α is the constant angular acceleration (rad/s²); θ is the angular displacement in that time (rad); t is the time (s).

items: Convert every speed to rad/s first: rad/s = rpm × 2π/60.
List ω₀, ω, α, θ, t and mark which one is unknown.
Pick the equation that holds the unknown and no other unknown.
Substitute with units, then check the sign of the answer against your convention.

sections.h3: Velocity and acceleration of a point at radius r

blocks.text: Take a point P at perpendicular distance r from the fixed axis. Its speed along its circle is v = ωr, directed along the tangent. This is why ω must be in rad/s. A shaft turning at 60 rpm has ω = 60 × 2π/60 = 6.283 rad/s, so a point at r = 0.5 m moves at 3.14 m/s, not 30 m/s.
v = ωr    a_t = αr    a_n = ω²r = v²/r
blocks.where: v is the speed along the tangent (m/s); a_t is the tangential acceleration (m/s²), along the tangent, changing the speed; a_n is the normal or centripetal acceleration (m/s²), directed towards the axis, changing only the direction of the velocity; r is the perpendicular distance from the axis (m); ω is in rad/s; α is in rad/s².

blocks.text: The two acceleration parts are perpendicular, so the total acceleration has magnitude a = √(a_t² + a_n²). A body spinning at steady speed has α = 0 and only a_n survives. A body starting from rest has ω = 0, so only a_t exists at that first instant.

These relations size real hardware: the rim stress in a flywheel grows with ω²r, bearings must carry the pull that a_n creates, and the safe working speed of a grinding wheel is set by a_n at its rim.

figure.caption: The two simple motions a rigid body can have, and the two acceleration parts of a point at radius r on a rotating body. Both acceleration parts come from the same rotation, one from α and one from ω.

spec.title: Rigid-body motion
spec.aria: A rigid body's motion splits into translation and fixed-axis rotation; rotation gives a tangential acceleration αr and a normal acceleration ω²r at radius r.

examples.question: A flywheel starts from rest with constant angular acceleration α = 2.5 rad/s². Find its angular velocity and its angular displacement after t = 4.0 s. At that instant, find the tangential and normal accelerations of a point 0.30 m from the axis.
steps: Data: ω₀ = 0 rad/s (starts from rest), α = 2.5 rad/s², t = 4.0 s, r = 0.30 m.
Angular velocity: ω = ω₀ + αt = 0 + 2.5 × 4.0 = 10 rad/s.
Angular displacement: θ = ω₀t + ½αt² = 0 + 0.5 × 2.5 × (4.0)² = 0.5 × 2.5 × 16 = 20 rad, which is 20/(2π) ≈ 3.2 turns.
Check with the third equation: ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ gives 10² = 0 + 2 × 2.5 × 20 = 100. Both sides are 100, so the values agree.
Tangential acceleration: a_t = αr = 2.5 × 0.30 = 0.75 m/s², along the tangent.
Normal acceleration: a_n = ω²r = (10)² × 0.30 = 100 × 0.30 = 30 m/s², directed towards the axis.
Total acceleration: a = √(0.75² + 30²) = √(0.5625 + 900) = √900.56 = 30.01 m/s², almost entirely towards the axis.
examples.answer: ω = 10 rad/s, θ = 20 rad (about 3.2 turns), a_t = 0.75 m/s² along the tangent and a_n = 30 m/s² towards the axis.
examples.check:
alpha = 2.5
t = 4.0
r = 0.30
w0 = 0.0
w = w0 + alpha*t
theta = w0*t + 0.5*alpha*t*t
at = alpha*r
an = w*w*r
print(w)
print(theta)
print(at)
print(an)

traps: Feeding ω in degrees per second or rpm straight into v = ωr. Convert first: rad/s = rpm × 2π/60.
Reporting only a_t and forgetting a_n = ω²r. In the example a_n is 40 times larger than a_t, so the omission is badly wrong.
Mixing degrees and radians in ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ; the equation only holds when α is in rad/s² and θ in rad.
Ignoring the sign of α for a slowing wheel. Its α is opposite to ω, and using +α gives an absurd ω.
Confusing the body's ω, which is the same for all points, with a point's linear velocity, which grows with r.

quiz.q: Define angular velocity and angular acceleration of a rigid body in fixed-axis rotation, with units.
quiz.a: Angular velocity ω = dθ/dt, the rate of change of angular displacement, in rad/s. Angular acceleration α = dω/dt = d²θ/dt², in rad/s². Both are the same for every point of the body.

quiz.q: Write the three constant-α equations of rotation.
quiz.a: ω = ω₀ + αt; θ = ω₀t + ½αt²; ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ, with ω in rad/s, α in rad/s², θ in rad and t in s.

quiz.q: Two points on a rotating disc are at radii 0.10 m and 0.40 m. Compare their angular velocities and their linear speeds, and say why.
quiz.a: Both share the same ω, θ and α because they belong to one rigid body. Their speeds differ by v = ωr, so the outer point moves four times faster. The outer point covers a longer arc in the same time.

quiz.q: A wheel spinning at 300 rpm is brought to rest in 5.0 s with constant angular acceleration. Find α and the number of turns made.
A shaft starts from rest with α = 3.0 rad/s². For a point 0.20 m from the axis, find a_t and a_n at t = 2.0 s.
At t = 0 a pulley has ω = 10 rad/s anticlockwise and constant α = 4.0 rad/s² clockwise. When does it stop, and what happens after that?
quiz.a: Take anticlockwise positive: ω₀ = +10 rad/s, α = −4.0 rad/s². Setting ω = 0 gives t = ω₀/(−α) = 10/4.0 = 2.5 s. The displacement to that point is θ = 10 × 2.5 − ½ × 4.0 × 2.5² = 12.5 rad. After 2.5 s the pulley reverses and spins clockwise, still with α = −4.0 rad/s².

quiz.q: Can a point of a rotating rigid body have zero total acceleration while the body spins? Explain.
quiz.a: Only if the point lies on the axis, where r = 0. For any r > 0 the normal part a_n = ω²r is positive whenever ω ≠ 0, even if α = 0 and a_t = 0. So an off-axis point always accelerates towards the axis; that inward acceleration is what keeps it on its circle.

quiz.q: A book slides down a straight ramp without turning. Is it in translation? Give one more example of translation along a curved path.
quiz.a: Yes. Every line on the book keeps its direction, so every point has the same velocity and acceleration. A cabin on a Ferris wheel translates along a curved path: its centre moves on a circle but the cabin stays upright and does not rotate.

beyond: Not for the exam. Machine design uses these relations for the rim stress of a spinning flywheel, which grows roughly as ρω²r², and that is why high-speed flywheels for grid storage use carbon fibre and spin in vacuum. Rotor dynamics studies what happens when ω passes a shaft's critical speed and the shaft begins to whirl. Robotics treats this fixed-axis case as the model of a single joint before moving on to three-dimensional rotation. Search 'flywheel energy storage', 'rotor critical speed' or 'rigid body rotation about a fixed axis' to go further.
